subject: Modelling measurement bias in a hierarchical Bayesian model

messages.author: ffa9d79601717d80
messages.subject: Modelling measurement bias in a hierarchical Bayesian model
parts:
Dear Stan users and developers,

I'm working on the following hierarchical model. I have data Y[K,T] (K time series of length T), and my model has the form Y(k,t) ~ N(m(k,t), sigma_Y) with m(k,t) = f(t | phi(k)). Here the function f is a nonlinear function of time t parameterised by a vector phi(k). The phi(k) are hierarchical -- I assume phi(k) ~ lognormal(mu, sigma), as in my model there is the physical constraint phi(k) > 0.

Below is my Stan code of this model. This works just fine.

data {
  int<lower=0> K; // size of cross section
  int<lower=0> T; // length of time series
  int x[T]; // time variable
  real Y[K,T];
}


parameters{
  real<lower=0> sigma_Y;
  real mu[4];
  real<lower=0> sigma[4];
  real<lower=0> phi[K,4];
}


model {
  sigma_Y ~ cauchy(0,1);
  mu ~ normal(-2, 4);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  for (k in 1:K) {
    real m[T];
    for (j in 1:3) {
      phi[k,j] ~ lognormal(mu[j], sigma[j]);
    }
    phi[k,4] ~ lognormal(mu[4], 0.1*sigma[4]);
    for (t in 1:T) {
      m[t] <- phi[k,1] * exp(-phi[k,2] * exp(-phi[k,3]*x[t]) - phi[k,4]*x[t]);
    }
    Y[k] ~ normal(m, sigma_Y);
  }
}

Unfortunately, the data I have is not Y, but a measurement Y_obs. This measurement is not perfect: according to some estimates we measure Y_obs = Y for about 30% of the observations, and Y_obs < Y for the remaining 70%. In general we can write Y_obs(k,t) = Y(k,t) * coverage(k,t), with coverage(k,t) having a distribution between 0 and 1. In essence the problem is that Y_obs is, on average, a biased measurement of Y. I have some information that I can use to formulate a prior distribution for coverage, but not nearly enough information to be certain. I want to make inferences on phi which reflect this uncertainty. 

A simple first step,I thought, would be to assume a fixed distribution for coverage, but I have difficulties implementing this in Stan. If I do something like Y_obs/Y_real ~ Beta(a,b) with fixed a, b, the sampler gets in trouble when it gets to a part of the parameter space where Y_obs/Y_real > 1 (if I interpret the error message correctly). Another try involved modelling Y_obs(k,t) ~ N(m(k,t) * coverage(k,t), sigma_Y), with coverage(k,t) ~ Beta(a,b). Here the problem is that I have to constrain coverage(k,t) to the interval [0,1], which I can only do if I declare all the coverage(k,n) parameters in the parameters block, which means Stan will save K*N (>10000) extra parameters in each iteration.

Any ideas?

If I do something like Y_obs/Y_real ~ Beta(a,b) with fixed a, b, the sampler gets in trouble when it gets to a part of the parameter space where Y_obs/Y_real > 1 (if I interpret the error message correctly).

If you truly always measure Y_obs < Y_real, then you need to constrain Y_real.
The problem with this is that Stan doesn't let you specify varying constraints,
so you have to code it up yourself (possible, just some work --- declare
an unconstrained parameter Y_real_offset and define Y_real <- Y_obs + Y_real_offset.
It's a simple linear transform, so the nice part is you don't incur any Jacobian
with this transfer

parameters {
matrix<lower=0>[K,T] y_real_unobs;

model {
matrix[K,T] y_real;
y_real <- y_real_unobs + y;

... whatever you would've done with y_real ...

}

So now y_real_unobs is the number of unobserved items. The lower bound of 0
means you won't get exactly 0 unless there's numerical underflow.

Also, given that y_real is a parameter, you have to be careful to apply the Jacobian
adjustment when you take

(y_obs / y_real) ~ Beta(a,b);

if you want to get the right distribution on Y_real.

> Another try involved modelling Y_obs(k,t) ~ N(m(k,t) * coverage(k,t), sigma_Y), with coverage(k,t) ~ Beta(a,b). Here the problem is that I have to constrain coverage(k,t) to the interval [0,1], which I can only do if I declare all the coverage(k,n) parameters in the parameters block, which means Stan will save K*N (>10000) extra parameters in each iteration.
>
> Any ideas?
>

Either way, you get a latent parameter for each observation
by declaring y_real.

You can't write

coverage[k,t] ~ beta(a,b);

unless coverage is defined as a parameter (or a constant or a function
of some other parameter). The sampling statement doesn't literally sample,
it just increments the log density.

- Bob

So now y_real_unobs is the number of unobserved items.  The lower bound of 0
means you won't get exactly 0 unless there's numerical underflow.

Thanks a lot -- didn't know this trick.

Let me explain a bit how the measurement errors occur. The data I have is collected from a push-based data feed which logs each occurence of a certain event (I don't want to get into too much detail by explaining what the event is). This was then aggregated to a daily total count per country. The data I have are weekly averages of these daily counts, for a period of 5 years. During these 5 years, the server delivering the data was not very stable -- think of issues like technical malfunction, full hard drives, server maintenance etc. I don't have the original data or meta-data about these technical issues -- just the weekly averages. Looking at the data I can see some large drops in weekly averages, and I estimate the weekly averages are affected about 70% of the time, to varying degrees.

Does anyone here have any experience with data like this? I'm not too excited about introducing a Beta(a,b) distributed latent parameter for every observation in the dataset (>100000 obs), as things will be too slow and unstable (based on some tests with small subsamples of the data).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modelling measurement bias in a hierarchical Bayesian model
parts:
Thanks --- that's very clear. And presumably the malfunctions
all result in underreporting --- there aren't malfunctions like
events being double counted or decimal point misplacement (like
you get in many financial data feeds).

I don't have any experience with such models and don't
know how to introduce measurement error without introducing
a parameter per observation. Others might have ideas.

Speed and stability in Stan (and MCMC in general) are greatly
affected by parameterization and by priors, as they both affect
the curvature in the posterior. So it might be possible to take
other measures to speed things up.

- Bob
